title: Flights from the UK to Reykjavik, Iceland: Costs and When to Go
subtitle: A 4-day trip costs £800-£1,200 per person. Here's where the money goes and why it's still worth it.
airport_names: London Heathrow, London Luton, London Gatwick, Manchester, Edinburgh
meta: Flights from UK airports to Reykjavik, Iceland: who flies there, today's cheapest fares, what a 4-day trip really costs, and the best months for the Northern Lights.

sections.heading: The flights: who flies where from the UK
sections.body:
Icelandair from Heathrow is the most comfortable option, with return fares often around £95-£180 outside peak dates. The flight takes about three hours, you get a free carry-on and a personal item, and the planes are decent. Prices sit nearer £220-£320 in July and over Christmas.

easyJet fly to Keflavik from Gatwick and Luton, with return fares that can drop to around £55-£130 outside summer. The catch is the bags. Add a cabin case and a seat and your cheap £70 flight turns into £130 quickly, so price the full lot before you click.

Wizz Air have run Keflavik routes from Luton in recent years, with fares from around £40-£90 each way when they appear. Check the current schedule before you plan around it, because Wizz routes to Iceland have come and gone. Icelandair also fly from Manchester and Edinburgh from around £140-£260 return, which saves a trek south if you live up north.

One thing nobody mentions: Keflavik is 45 minutes from Reykjavik. The Flybus costs about £25-£30 return, and a taxi will run you £120-£150 one way. Take the bus.

sections.heading: What it really costs: the honest budget
sections.body:
A 4-day trip lands at £800-£1,200 per person all-in, and anyone telling you £500 is either camping or lying. Flights £100-£250, a double room in Reykjavik £130-£220 a night split between two, and that's before you eat anything.

Food is where it stings. A basic burger and chips is £18-£22, a pint is £9-£11, and a sit-down dinner with a drink is £35-£55 a head. The easy saving is the supermarkets: Bonus, the one with the yellow pig logo, sells sandwiches and snacks for a fraction of café prices, which leaves room for one proper dinner out.

Then the tours. The Golden Circle with a coach company is £60-£90, a Northern Lights tour is £70-£100, and the Blue Lagoon is £65-£110 depending on the package and the date. Add a hire car at £50-£120 a day plus petrol at roughly £2 a litre and it climbs fast.

Why bother, then? Because nowhere else in Europe looks like this. Waterfalls the size of office blocks, black sand beaches, steaming ground you can walk on. You're paying for scenery you can't get anywhere else, and for many people that's worth more than a week of beach days in Spain for the same money.

sections.heading: Northern Lights: when to go and how to see them
sections.body:
The aurora is luck, not a guarantee, and the season runs roughly September to March. Plenty of trips get cloud one night and only a faint green smear the next, so give yourself several nights rather than pinning everything on one.

Reykjavik is the worst place to see it. The street lights wash everything out, so you need to get away from the city, ideally an hour or more out, onto a dark road with a clear sky. Check vedur.is for the cloud forecast and the aurora forecast, and ignore anyone promising 100% sightings.

Book a tour on your first night, not your last, because most operators let you rebook free if it's cancelled. That gives you extra shots at it. A coach tour is £70-£100, a small-group minibus is £100-£150, and hiring a car and chasing it yourself costs nothing extra if you're already driving.

Wrap up properly. Standing in a field at midnight in February can mean minus five with wind, and thin gloves won't last ten minutes. Proper thermals, a windproof, a flask of something hot.

When to go, month by month. The aurora season runs from about late August to mid-April, whenever the sky is dark enough. September and March, around the equinoxes, are often lively and give you milder weather and longer days for sightseeing. October to February has the longest nights. December is the darkest month but also the stormiest, so January and February are a good balance of dark skies and enough daylight to explore.

Plan around the moon and the weather. A bright full moon washes out fainter displays, so the week either side of a new moon gives the best odds. Clear skies matter more than anything, and Icelandic weather turns quickly, so give yourself at least three nights rather than one.

Book winter flights early. February half-term and the weeks around Christmas and New Year sell out first. Midweek departures in November, January and early March are usually the cheapest way to get a winter trip with good aurora odds. The table above shows today's cheapest fares from each UK airport.

sections.heading: Summer vs winter, and the Ring Road question
sections.body:
Summer gives you 20 hours of daylight and every road open, but prices peak at £250-£320 return from Heathrow and rooms jump 40-60%. You get puffins, midnight sun and the full Highlands. You don't get the aurora, because it's simply too light.

Winter gives you the lights, ice caves and cheaper flights from around £95-£180, but daylight is four to five hours in December and roads close without warning. January and February are the sweet spot, with enough light to drive and decent aurora odds. Book a car with proper winter tyres and read the road.is warnings every morning.

The Ring Road is 1,330km and the honest answer is no, not in four days. Do it properly in 7-10 days or you'll spend the whole trip staring through a windscreen. You're better off doing the south coast, Golden Circle and one glacier lagoon well than rushing the lot.

For four days, base yourself in Reykjavik, then do the south coast out to Vik with Seljalandsfoss, Skogafoss and Reynisfjara black beach. Add the Golden Circle, one geothermal bath that isn't the Blue Lagoon, and an aurora night. That's a trip you'll talk about for years, even if your bank balance won't thank you.
